    <div class="content-inner">

    <div class="headline">Predicting Employee Churn</div>

    <div class="project-meta-block">
      <p class="project-meta-line">UC Irvine &middot; MSBA Coursework</p>
      <p class="project-meta-line">09/2025-12/2025</p>
    </div>

    <p class="body-text"><strong>Project Context:</strong> Employee turnover imposes substantial costs on organizations through lost expertise, productivity disruptions, and recruitment and training expenses. For this BANA 273 machine learning project, my team analyzed a <a href="https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/tejashvi14/employee-future-prediction" target="_blank">publicly available Kaggle dataset</a> of 4,653 employees across three major Indian cities to identify which employee characteristics most strongly predict voluntary churn, an employee leaving on their own, and to build a model capable of flagging at-risk employees early enough for targeted intervention.</p>

    <p class="body-text"><strong>Business Question:</strong> <em>Which employee attributes and organizational factors most strongly influence churn, and how accurately can they be used to identify at-risk employees?</em></p>

    <div class="mobile-cta-row">
      <a class="dashboard-mobile-link" href="report.pdf" target="_blank">Full Report &rarr;</a>
      <a class="dashboard-mobile-link" href="slides.pdf" target="_blank">Slides &rarr;</a>
      <a class="dashboard-mobile-link" href="code.html" target="_blank">Code &rarr;</a>
    </div>

    <div class="tabs">
      <button class="tab-btn active" onclick="showTab('findings', this)">Findings</button>
      <button class="tab-btn" onclick="showTab('recommendations', this)">Recommendations</button>
      <button class="tab-btn" onclick="showTab('methodology-takeaways', this)">Methodology &amp; Takeaways</button>
    </div>

    <!-- FINDINGS -->
    <div id="findings" class="tab-panel active">
      <div class="section-heading" style="margin-top:0.25rem;">Who Is Most Likely to Leave?</div>
      <ul class="findings-list">
        <li><strong>Mid-pay tier employees churn the most,</strong> at 2.2x the odds of low-pay employees, sharpest when pay feels neither entry-level nor rewarding.</li>
        <li><strong>Master's degree holders churn 2.4x more than Bachelor's holders,</strong> likely reflecting greater external mobility and a mismatch with available advancement.</li>
        <li><strong>Benched employees, those without a current project assignment, churn 1.5x more</strong> than employees who have never been benched.</li>
        <li><strong>Pune employees churn 1.6x more than Bangalore employees,</strong> pointing to regional labor market or workplace differences.</li>
        <li><strong>Female employees show a higher churn rate than male employees,</strong> consistent across both descriptive analysis and the model.</li>
      </ul>

      <div class="section-heading" style="margin-top: 2rem;">Model Performance</div>
      <p class="prose">Two models were compared on recall (the share of actual churners correctly caught), the priority metric since missing a churner costs far more than a false alarm.</p>
      <div class="model-grid">
        <div class="model-card">
          <div class="model-card-title">Logistic Regression</div>
          <div class="model-card-recall">63%</div>
          <div class="model-card-label">Recall (Churn Class)</div>
          <div class="model-card-desc">Identified education, pay tier, city, benching, and gender as the strongest predictors, with strong interpretability through odds ratios.</div>
        </div>
        <div class="model-card winner">
          <div class="model-card-title">Tuned Decision Tree</div>
          <div class="model-card-recall">79%</div>
          <div class="model-card-label">Recall (Churn Class)</div>
          <div class="model-card-desc">Joining year and pay tier were the dominant splits, capturing nonlinear interactions the logistic model can't.</div>
        </div>
      </div>
      <p class="prose">The two models tell complementary stories: logistic regression surfaces linear trends and effect sizes, while the decision tree reveals how tenure, pay, and education combine into risk pathways neither variable alone would predict.</p>
    </div>

    <!-- RECOMMENDATIONS -->
    <div id="recommendations" class="tab-panel">

      <div class="rec-card high">
        <div class="rec-priority">High Priority</div>
        <div class="rec-title">Target Long-Tenured Mid-Pay Employees First</div>
        <div class="rec-segment">Primary risk group across both models</div>
        <div class="rec-desc">Joining year and pay tier were the two dominant predictors of churn. Concentrate outreach, career-development conversations, and pay adjustments on longer-tenured, mid-pay employees before turnover occurs.</div>
      </div>

      <div class="rec-card high">
        <div class="rec-priority">High Priority</div>
        <div class="rec-title">Review Mid-Tier Compensation Structure</div>
        <div class="rec-segment">Mid-pay tier &middot; 19.7% of employees, 2.2x churn odds</div>
        <div class="rec-desc">Mid-tier dissatisfaction was the most consistent finding across both models. A pay equity analysis with clearer promotion pathways could close the gap between contribution and compensation driving this.</div>
      </div>

      <div class="rec-card med">
        <div class="rec-priority">Medium Priority</div>
        <div class="rec-title">Minimize Bench Time and Improve Communication During Gaps</div>
        <div class="rec-segment">Ever-benched employees &middot; 10.3% of workforce, 1.5x churn odds</div>
        <div class="rec-desc">Reducing unassigned periods where possible, and proactively communicating during unavoidable bench time, can reduce the sense of exclusion it appears to create.</div>
      </div>

      <div class="rec-card med">
        <div class="rec-priority">Medium Priority</div>
        <div class="rec-title">Develop Location-Specific Retention Programs for Pune</div>
        <div class="rec-segment">Pune employees &middot; 1.6x churn odds vs Bangalore</div>
        <div class="rec-desc">Retention strategy shouldn't be uniform across cities. Compensation benchmarks and engagement programs should be evaluated and tailored specifically for the Pune workforce.</div>
      </div>

      <div class="rec-card low">
        <div class="rec-priority">Lower Priority</div>
        <div class="rec-title">Create Advancement Pathways for Highly Educated Employees</div>
        <div class="rec-segment">Master's degree holders &middot; 18.8% of workforce, 2.4x churn odds</div>
        <div class="rec-desc">Master's holders churn at more than double the rate of Bachelor's employees. Clearer recognition and advancement tracks can close the gap between expectation and reality driving this.</div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <!-- METHODOLOGY & TAKEAWAYS -->
    <div id="methodology-takeaways" class="tab-panel">

      <div class="section-heading" style="margin-top:0.25rem;">Methodology</div>
      <ul class="findings-list">
        <li><strong>Data prep:</strong> 4,653 records across 9 attributes from Kaggle, no missing values; categorical variables one-hot encoded for logistic regression, used directly by the decision tree; 70/30 train-test split, random state 42.</li>
        <li><strong>Class imbalance:</strong> 65.6% of employees stay, only 34.4% churn, so both models used balanced class weighting and recall became the primary evaluation metric instead of accuracy.</li>
        <li><strong>Modeling:</strong> logistic regression improved via GridSearchCV (L1 regularization) from 0.41 to 0.63 recall; the decision tree, pre-pruned and with its classification threshold (the probability cutoff for flagging a churner) lowered from 0.50 to 0.35, reached 0.79 recall. Both were confirmed stable via 5-fold cross-validation.</li>
      </ul>

      <div class="section-heading">Takeaways</div>
      <ul class="findings-list">
        <li>Choosing the right evaluation metric mattered more than choosing the right model. Once recall replaced accuracy, a model that looked decent was actually catching fewer than half the churners it needed to find.</li>
        <li>Threshold tuning is an underused lever. Lowering the cutoff from 0.50 to 0.35 lifted the tree's recall from 0.64 to 0.79 with no additional feature engineering.</li>
        <li>The clearest output of a churn model isn't the model itself, it's the ranked list of risk factors it produces. Tenure, pay tier, education, and location each point to a concrete HR intervention a manager can actually act on.</li>
      </ul>

    </div>
